prompt.context: Bain is serving a private equity client thinking of purchasing a fresh fruit juice manufacturer. The company operates on the West Coast and serves the high end health food market. Currently servings are in 16 oz bottles. The juice is sold in high-end delis, cafes such as Starbucks, and large upscale grocery chains such as Whole Foods. Last year they had $90 million in revenues and they have been growing at 15% for the past 3 years. They have strong sales and marketing teams and a strong brand name.
prompt.question: The private equity company wants us to identify whether the company is an attractive acquisition. What are some things you would look into?

clarifying_info.q: Are the two top players only operating on the west coast or are they nationwide?
clarifying_info.a: The two top players operate nationwide. They have been in the market for longer than the acquisition target.

clarifying_info.q: Does the PE client have anything in their portfolio that could generate synergies?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they own a low end soda and bottled water manufacturer that makes private labels in the US and Canada. The private labels are sold at retailers like Walmart and CostCo.

clarifying_info.q: What are the competitor prices for similar juice products?

exhibits.title: Industry and Company Context
exhibits.shows: Page containing key insight notes about the target's competitive position and Phase 3 private equity fit discussion
exhibits.data: Target is #3 in market; top 2 players hold 70% of $1B market; market growing at 10% annually; target growing at 15%

exhibits.title: Profitability Analysis
exhibits.shows: Page containing cost structure data and profitability calculation
exhibits.data: COGS $0.75/bottle; manufacturing 20% of revenue; sales & marketing $15M; distribution $30M; selling price $2.50/bottle; revenue $90M

framework: Industry dynamics: market size, growth rate, key drivers of purchases, trends, competitor market share, new entrants, customer segments
Margins / profitability: price per unit, cost structure of the firm vs. competitors, potential future changes in cost structure from external forces
Private Equity fit: is the acquisition price fair, is there a viable exit strategy, how does the target fit with current portfolio, are there synergies

questions.prompt: Phase 1 – How would you think about evaluating this acquisition opportunity?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure around three buckets: (1) industry dynamics (size, growth, competition), (2) company profitability and cost structure, and (3) PE fit including price, exit strategy, and portfolio synergies. Broad brainstorm acceptable here.

questions.prompt: Phase 2 – The high end juice market in the US is $1B. Our client is the third largest presence. The #1 and #2 players have 70% of the market. The market is growing at 10% annually. What are the one or two most relevant pieces of information you would like about the industry landscape?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates ask: (1) Are top players nationwide or regional? (2) Why have they captured such large share — longer tenure, better product? Key insight: the target has grown to #3 while competing only on the West Coast against national players. Its 15% growth vs. the industry's 10% suggests its product is competitive and expansion nationally could make it a major player.

questions.prompt: Phase 3 – The PE client owns a low end soda and bottled water manufacturer making private labels sold at Walmart and CostCo. Evaluate the potential synergies.
questions.guidance: Manufacturing synergies are limited — juice manufacturing uses different ingredients, processes, and quality standards than soda/water. Distribution channel synergies are risky: placing a high-end product in low-end retailers (Walmart/CostCo) would damage the brand image, and those retailers would use buyer power to push prices down. Sales and marketing competencies from the low-end business do not align with the high-end juice brand. Overall conclusion: the target looks promising standalone but there are no obvious synergies with the existing portfolio.

questions.prompt: Phase 4 – COGS are $0.75 per bottle, manufacturing is 20% of revenue, sales and marketing is $15M, distribution is $30M, and each bottle sells for $2.50. Analyze the company's profitability.
questions.guidance: Walk through each line item systematically. The company is breakeven — zero profit — despite strong revenue growth. This is the critical finding that frames the rest of the case.

math.setup: Revenue = $90M; bottles sold = $90M / $2.50 = 36M bottles. Calculate each cost line then sum.
math.answer: $0 profit — the company is exactly breaking even.

questions.prompt: Phase 4 continued – How would you go about improving profitability? First, what are ways to cut costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm cost reduction levers across the P&L.

questions.prompt: Phase 4 continued – What ideas do you have about increasing revenues?
questions.guidance: Candidate should ask about competitor pricing before suggesting price changes. Competitor price is also $2.50, so raising price would risk market share loss or a price war. Better lever: expand distribution channels (hotels, catering companies, restaurants) that align with the high-end brand image rather than discounting or aggressive pricing moves.

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways to cut costs for this fruit juice company?

categories.name: Procurement / COGS
ideas: Consolidate suppliers — centralize procurement to gain volume discounts
Negotiate better input pricing given growing scale

categories.name: Manufacturing
ideas: Automate factory operations to increase throughput and reduce labor cost
Eliminate less profitable juice flavors via SKU profitability analysis; reallocate shelf and production capacity to high-margin lines

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Change packaging to make it lighter without hurting brand image — reduces fuel and shipping costs

categories.name: SG&A / Headcount
ideas: Reduce headcount especially at senior levels where roles may overlap post-acquisition
Integrate sales and marketing spend more efficiently

recommendation: This is an attractive acquisition target overall
The company is growing at 15% — faster than the 10% industry rate — as the #3 player competing against larger national incumbents, signaling strong product quality and brand

It is currently breaking even ($0 profit) but has clear levers to improve margins: cost reduction (procurement consolidation, automation, lighter packaging, SKU rationalization) and revenue growth (channel expansion into hotels, restaurants, catering)
If the PE firm can execute on these levers and potentially expand the brand nationally, the upside is substantial
risks: No portfolio synergies exist with the current low-end soda/water business; the acquisition must stand on its own merits
Placing the brand in lower-end channels to chase volume could erode the premium positioning
Raising prices is not viable given competitive parity at $2.50 — margin improvement must come primarily from cost reduction
National expansion requires significant investment and carries execution risk against entrenched nationwide players
next_steps: Determine a fair acquisition price and assess exit strategy (e.g., strategic sale, IPO)
Model the financial impact of identified cost reduction initiatives
Evaluate feasibility and investment required for national geographic expansion
Conduct deeper due diligence on manufacturing operations and distribution contracts
